Enclosure and panel

An enclosure from sticks, panel holes, shunt and Q1, jacks, cables — sub-step by sub-step, each with its drawing and 3D view. At the end: which measurement you take from where.

What this document is — rules

  • The boards are done. From here on: an enclosure from sticks, panel holes, shunt and Q1, jacks, cables, tests.
  • Part info: in the drawings and the 3D view, hover over a part (tap on a phone): its name, size, for a stick its length and its row in the cut list, the step it is fitted in, and its place in stock. Click / tap: the card stays put. With the keyboard: in drawings Tab moves from part to part, in 3D N / P next / previous part, Esc closes.
  • The enclosure is made of tongue depressors (wooden sticks) (150 × 18 × 2 mm). Inside 214 × 154 × 90 mm, outside 222 × 162 × 94.
  • Strength: the walls are two layers (outside 5 horizontal rows, inside vertical sticks; 4 mm), a 6 × 18 mm post in each of the four corners; the lid comes off through the side walls with M3x12 bolts + nuts; the boards are screwed to feet with embedded nuts. Base and lid pieces come from the flat section: no rounded end ends up under a wall. Holes are made before the walls go up, while the piece lies on a flat surface.
  • Rule: valuable parts — the boards (A, B), ESP32, shunt, Q1 — are never glued (screws, feet, connectors); the enclosure's own parts (sticks, feet, spacers) are glued. Wall parts glued with hot glue (your decision): YUVA1 (hot glue), YUVA2 (hot glue), MT1 (hot glue), MT2 (hot glue), IZ (hot glue), CB (hot glue), KL (hot glue), F0 (hot glue), F1P (hot glue), F2 (hot glue) — they come off with isopropyl alcohol or a heat gun.
  • Limit of use: only battery / DC-DC powered circuits that float with respect to earth. No USB plugged in while measuring HV.
  • Below, go one at a time with next / back; the 3D view is under the step bar (drag: rotate, Ctrl+wheel: zoom). From a phone at the bench: python uretim/belge_sun.py.
  • Every step that uses sticks has a "Stick pieces needed in this step" table: how many of which length, drawn on the stick. 1.2 and 4.4 are the combined cut lists; their "which step" column gives the same information.

Which glue goes where

JobGlueHow
Laminated (stacked) parts: foot blocks, posts, corner bracket, anchor, TP4056 shelf blocksCA glue (super glue, liquid)A thin line on the face, press 30 s; no clamp needed. Do not drip it into the thread of the embedded nut — fit the nut dry.
Base / lid rows (end to end and side by side)Masking tape + CA glueLay the pieces out on a flat surface, hold them from above with masking tape and run thin CA glue into the joints (put Kapton / baking paper underneath: it sticks to the table).
Rails (under the base, under the lid)Hot glueA continuous thin bead along the rail; press within 10 s. The only glue that gives you time to adjust the position.
Outer layer rows (to the base and to each other)CA glue + hot glue from insideTack the ends and the middle with CA glue (align, press 30 s), then run a hot-glue fillet into the inside corner: the CA gives the alignment, the hot glue the strength.
Inner layer vertical sticksCA glue (three lines: top, middle, bottom)Hot glue adds thickness (the inner layer must be 2 mm, otherwise the holes no longer line up); CA stays thin. Put the stick in the right place the first time — there is no room to slide it.
Shunt / ESP32 spacers (to the base)Hot glueEnclosure parts; if they ever need to come off, cut underneath with a utility knife.
ESP32 cradle (side rails, shoulder blocks — on top of the spacer)CA glue (super glue, liquid)With the devkit in place and a layer of paper wrapped around its edge, press the piece against it, a drop of CA glue, press 30 s. Do not let CA glue touch the devkit; pull the paper out once it has cured.
18650 holders, modules (MT1, MT2, B0505S), 680 µF, KL, fuse strips (inner face of the back wall)Hot glueTwo beads along the full length of the holder's base, press against the wall 10 s; where it lands between the inner-layer sticks, leave the glue thick (it fills the 2 mm gap). NOT CA glue: it does not bond some holder plastics (PP) and turns brittle with heat. To remove: heat gun or isopropyl alcohol + utility knife.
Silicone sealant (tube, curing)DO NOT USENot structural, cures in 24 hours, nothing sticks on top of it. Only around the jack nuts if you later want water/dust sealing.
The shunt itself and the Kelvin solder jointsNo glue — heat-shrink + cable tieAt 9.5 A the shunt heats up by ~45 °C and in a closed box it goes past 70 °C: hot glue softens and flows at ~65 °C, and it also stops the shunt from cooling (the 9.5 A limit assumes cooling in open air). These joints are desoldered when changing to 15 mΩ. The strain is taken by a cable tie (7.2: the twisted pair to the shunt spacer); if you like, heat-shrink over the solder — leave the lower end of the leg that goes into the terminal block bare.
Places touching the heatsink itself (Q1's tab, the gate wire, the mica washer)Cable tie, no glueHot glue softens on the heatsink's surface; CA turns brittle with heat. ⚠ Gluing the corner bracket to the BASE is OUTSIDE this ban (6.6): that joint is 16 mm of wood away from the heatsink, the heat that reaches it is under 1 K.

POWER (GÜÇ)
front · x 71 · z 81		Ø5.05 mm LED, green (clear)
LED003 · LED-Mekanik Kutusu		The ONLY visual answer to whether the board is powered. It has to be on the +12 rail: the current flows INTO GND, i.e. the direction 7912 is designed to sink. Placed between GND and −12 it would ask the regulator to SOURCE current, which a 79xx cannot do. An indicator driven by the ESP32 would lie 'ready' while the ESP32 is on USB and the analog side is off — hence passive.

front · x 143 · z 81		Ø8.04 mm banana jack, clear black (large)
CON027 · Soketler 1 Kutusu		B60 (user decision, nothing to buy): CAL is a BLACK large jack — stock has 2 of each colour, yellow is reserved for HV. It can be confused with COM but it is HARMLESS: a COM lead plugged into CAL does not start a measurement, 22 kΩ burns nothing. In B59 it moved to the top right, next to SCOPE and above V: the CAL → SCOPE patch lead is short. In the user's sketch it sat right above HV — an HV probe (614 V) slipping into CAL would push ~28 mA through 22 kΩ and kill the GPIO and both ADS chips; it swapped places with SCOPE. Its neighbours are V and SCOPE, the closest 22 mm away.

Lid bolts ×4Ø3.2M3x12 + nut + washer (MEK034/035)Through the side walls (y 45 / 117, z 81) into the lid rail; no thread is cut in the wood, the nut holds → the lid comes on and off. THE RAIL IS DRILLED TOO (13.1): the hole in the wall serves as a guide, same Ø3.2.

Layer 4 below the pocket also gets a Ø3.2 hole — so the screw tip does not bottom out; <b>the layers below are not drilled</b> (board A block 9 layers, board B block 4 layers). The TP1 module has NO mounting hole: it is held to a wooden holder with a cable tie. No holes at all are made in the wall for wall parts.

Positions are inner coordinates (seen from the front, from the left); the part-by-part table in 3.1/3.2 measures the same holes from the part's own end. All jacks are the same model (large clear, B60). Colours: red = V/SCOPE, black = COM and CAL, YELLOW = HV only, blue = BATTERY, green = LOAD.

How do I make the holes (without a drill)

StageHow
MarkWith a ruler measure x from the left end of the piece and z from its bottom edge, draw two lines; where they cross is the CENTRE of the hole. Without compasses, mark the diameter/2 and draw a small circle (3.25 mm for Ø6.5).
PilotPress an awl / thick needle / nail point into the centre gently and twist to make a 1–2 mm dimple. NO HAMMERING — a driven nail splits a 2 mm stick along the grain.
Piercing (soldering iron)Press an old conical tip of the soldering iron (350 °C) square onto the centre; it gets through 2 mm of wood in 5–10 s and burns a ~3 mm hole. Put a scrap stick underneath, open the window (smoke). It does not split the wood — the safest way without a drill. The burnt edge ends up under the jack's flange/nut.
Drilling (drill bit by hand)If you have drill bits, a 3 mm bit held in pliers and turned by hand also gets through (2 mm of wood, ~1 min). A hand drill / pin vise (100–200 ₺) brings the M3 holes down to a minute — for Ø6–8 you still need to enlarge.
EnlargingBring the 3 mm hole up to size by twisting the tip of a utility knife or with 120 sandpaper wrapped around a pen/marker: <b>for Ø5 a knife tip or sandpaper wrapped around a screwdriver shaft</b> (only 2 mm bigger than the ~3 mm the iron makes), for Ø6 a pen, for Ø8 a thick marker. Test often with the jack: the body should go through with friction, with no play (then the jack does not turn when the nut is tightened). <b>Ventilation holes (Ø5) are the exception:</b> no tight fit needed there, the hole just has to be open — the LED, however, must fit tightly or it falls out the front.
The largest hole (Ø8) — the thinnest woodThe largest round hole on the panel is Ø8: on a 18 mm stick that leaves <b>5.0 mm</b> of wood on each side — the easiest place to crack. Enlarge with sandpaper wrapped around a thick marker, test often with the jack, put a scrap stick underneath. If you later need a bigger hole than a pen/marker can enlarge: draw the circle, burn 8–10 small holes <b>ON the circle</b> with the iron, push the centre out with a knife, file up to the line.
Oval slot (14 × 9)Draw two Ø9 circles at ±2.5 mm from the centre (centres 5 mm apart), open both with the iron + enlarging, cut straight between them with a utility knife, round off the corners. The metal shell of a USB-C / Type-C plug is 8.5 × 2.6, its plastic overmould ~12 × 6.5: 14 × 9 lets it through easily.
M3 holes (Ø3.2)One pass with the iron tip is enough; the bolt should go through with friction. The Ø6.5 nut pocket in layers 2–3 of the foot and lid blocks: iron + enlarging, testing with the nut. <b>The layer right below the pocket</b> also gets a Ø3.2 hole (so the screw tip does not bottom out); the layers further down are not drilled.
Perfboard (FR4) — Ø3.2⚠ <b>DO NOT use the soldering iron:</b> glass fibre does not melt, the resin carbonises and carbon conducts. The empty 2×2 area in the board's corner already has Ø1 holes; <b>enlarge the middle hole</b>: <b>hold a 3 mm drill bit in pliers and turn it by hand</b> (~30 s in 1.6 mm FR4) or open it with a round needle file. Lay the board flat on the table with scrap wood underneath, do not press — the board cracks. <b>The dust is glass fibre:</b> wipe it with a damp cloth, do not blow. Board A is soldered: first check by eye that there are no traces or parts around the hole (the layout plan left that 2×2 empty).
Inner layer (5.1)The hole in the outer layer is the guide: pass the iron tip through it to pierce the inner stick, then enlarge. Behind the oval slots the inner stick is short, no drilling.
CheckPiece on a flat surface: any cracks (hold it up to the light)? Does the jack nut sit flat? If cracked, fill with CA glue and press before it cures; if the crack is large, cut the piece again (there are spares).

All hole dimensions are to the centre of the hole. Diameter column Ø = round hole; "14 × 9 oval" = width × height rectangular slot (USB, CHARGE). Round: banana jacks Ø6.5 / Ø8, toggles Ø6, M3 bolts Ø3.2.

Materials — from stock 23, to buy 3

Take from stock

WhatRecordNote
Test leads (banana + alligator clip)CON065, CON066 · Soketler 1 KutusuThe calibration steps (12.2–12.7) need leads to the panel jacks: one end a 4 mm male banana plug (CON005/CON006, 4 pcs), the other an alligator clip (CON065/066, 10 pcs) — both in stock. A short banana–banana lead for CAL → SCOPE is made from the same parts.
50 mA 5×20 glass fuse (fast, F — the one in stock)FUS010 · Sigortalar KutusuMeasure one: a genuine 50 mA wire has a cold resistance of 15–21 Ω (Littelfuse 217/218); the 0.4 Ω in the holder = 400 mA (FUS001). An F 50 mA blows on the switch surge → keep the 400 mA in the holder until the T type below arrives (none of the F fuses in stock gives ≥3× margin on the surge).
Heatsink bleed resistor: 1 MΩR026, R039 · Direnç KutusuQ1's heatsink is insulated with mica, i.e. a floating metal plate inside the box. It is tied to board GND through 1 MΩ: static drains away, but if the mica is punctured it does not short BATTERY 1 to GND (38 µA). DO NOT use a plain wire.
Cell fuse ×2 (F1P, F2): 2 A F 5×20 glassFUS004 · Sigortalar KutusuOne on the POSITIVE end of each cell. The TP4056's protection FET (FS8205) sits between B−/OUT−, so the DW01A cannot interrupt a short on the cell end or in the H+/H− wire; only this fuse protects that branch (short-circuit 42 A). ⚠ Why the rating is high: the fuse is on the TP4056's BAT terminal, so the whole CHARGE current (1.00 A, factory Rprog setting) flows through it — a smaller one blows on the first charge. Continuous discharge 1161 mA; it is the charging that decides.
Fuse holder ×3: 5×20 PCB clips (F1P, F2, F0)FUS009 · Sigortalar KutusuOn the back wall, held to a stick piece with a cable tie (F1P to the right of the TP4056 shelf, F2 in the bottom right corner, F0 at the left end next to MT1). NO panel hole — inside the box, the lid is opened for service (changing a cell needs the lid opened anyway).
Q1 heatsink (the plan ASSUMES 15 × 40 × 42 mm)MEK002 · Soğutucu KutusuThe inventory has no size (MEK002 'various sizes'). The plan assumes 15 × 40 × 42 mm and reserved that space for Q1. If your block is bigger it still fits, but the clearance to board B shrinks — then make the block smaller or move Q1 2–3 mm to the right. If it is smaller, no problem: Q1 dissipates 1.4 W in the battery test, this block is more than enough (even without a heatsink Tj 121 °C, limit 175).
TO-220 insulation (mica/plastic insulator + bushing)MEK041 · Soğutucu KutusuTo insulate Q1 from the heatsink; plastic insulators with/without a hole are also available (MEK037–040)
M3×10 / M3×12 screws, nuts, washersMEK034 · Vida KutusuBoard feet ×6, lid ×4, Q1 corner bracket ×1; embedded nuts ×10 (6 feet + 4 lid rail blocks). The 18650 holders are now glued (B57b), no bolts for them
2-way screw terminal block 5 mm (24 V internal connection)CON007 · Soketler 2 KutusuThe board's 24 V wires go here; the board comes out without desoldering
Female header (3-way + 1-way connector ends)CON018 · Soketler 4 KutusuCut for the shunt harness and the Q1 gate wire
XP128 10 mm terminal block (shunt legs + load cables)CON064 · Soketler 2 KutusuShunt legs (10–11 mm) into the poles; glued to the spacer stick, the shunt is swapped with a screwdriver
5 mΩ Ø1.6 shunt (fitted) + 15 mΩ Ø1 (spare, for mA work)R042 · Direnç Kutusu5 mΩ: 9.5 A continuous, 1.56 mA step. 15 mΩ (R044): 3.4 A, 0.52 mA step; calibration 12.2 uses both
18650 cell ×2 (battery pack, parallel)PWR005 · yeri kayıtta yokButton-top cell: the button touches in the spring holder; fit the MEK025 insulating ring. Connected in PARALLEL: at first insertion the two cell voltages must be within ±0.1 V (10.3)
18650 single holder ×2PWR004, PWR009 · Giriş Kabloları Kutusu / yeri kayıtta yokPWR004 (motorobit) or PWR007 (direnc.net); 80×21×21 MEASURED (B52d) — PWR009 is a PCB type, cannot be bolted to the wall
TP4056 protected Type-C ×1 (single charging input)MOD002 · Sensörler KutusuCharges both parallel cells together. Rprog 1.2 kΩ factory (1 A, ~0.5 A per cell) → with 2.4 kΩ, 0.5 A, the box heats up less (optional)
MT3608 boost converter ×2MOD012 · yeri kayıtta yokOne at 5.0 V (5 V bus: ESP32 + analog input), one at 24.0 V (analog, fed from the B0505S); set with no load in 10.1
5 mm green LED + 10 kΩ resistor (POWER lamp)LED003 · LED-Mekanik KutusuLED003 ×20, resistor R060 (10K) ×50 — both in stock. If you want it brighter, 4.7K (R015): 2.1 mA
KTS102 toggle ×1 (BATTERY, the box's only switch)SW024 · Switchler 1 Kutusu3 pins: the middle + one end are used (ON-OFF). 2 in stock, one is a spare. Confirm the common (middle) pin with an ohmmeter, do not heat the pin for long when soldering. Since B58 no KTS202 is needed
F0 fuse: 1 A 5×20 glass (fast)FUS003 · Sigortalar KutusuOn the 5 V input of the measurement side, inside the box (B58e). It only blows on an internal fault; if it does, open the lid, find the fault first (B0505S, MT2, board), then replace it
B0505S-2WR3 (2 W) isolated DC-DC, 5 V → 5 V (Hi-Link, motorobit) — NOT 1 WMOD013 · yeri kayıtta yokThe one part that separates the box's two grounds (B58): the analog 24 V comes from this module's isolated output. Continuous load 0.73 W = 37%; the manufacturer's minimum-load requirement of 10% is 28% at the lowest load. DO NOT BUY the 1 W version (B0505S-1WR3): enough for the continuous load (73%) but not at power-up — in current limit it pulls MT2's input to ~2 V and the board cannot reach 24 V (B58f simulation, sim3_kutu_besleme.py). 1500 VDC isolation, short-circuit protected; body 19.5 × 7 × 10, its place on the wall is reserved. 680 µF 16 V electrolytic ×1 (MT2 input, CB)C042 · Elektrolitik Kondansatör KutusuB58f simulation: 470 µF is enough for every model, 220 is not. In stock 2; 470 µF 10 V (C040) also works

HB950 2-pin barrier terminal block ×1 (power node)CON011 · Soketler 2 KutusuThe heavy LOAD/BATTERY cables join here, a single bridge goes to the XP128. Two or three untinned twisted ends fit under a barrier screw; when changing the shunt only the two XP128 screws are loosened

To buy

WhatNote
Tongue depressor sticksNeeded 131, on hand ~50; buy at least 81, 101 with spares
Heavy wire for the load path (≥1.5 mm²)If the KBL003 mixed hook-up wire has a heavy conductor, take it from there (strip and measure: bare conductor ≥ 1.4 mm for solid wire, ~1.6 mm for a stranded bundle). Ring lugs are NOT in stock and the plan does NOT REQUIRE them: a solder lug on the jack or an untinned loop between two nuts, an untinned twisted end in the barrier block (5.2). Buying lugs is optional: the barrel of an uninsulated lug is crimped and soldered.
50 mA T (time-delay) 5×20 glass fuse, branded — OPTIONAL, later planLittelfuse 218.050 / ESKA 522.5xx / Schurter; glass body (ceramic 50 mA has too much resistance). ≥ 10× margin on the switch-on surge (136 µF); a T 63 mA also works (more margin). User decision 2026-09-24: the fuse in the holder has never blown, the build does not expect it to.
3D view left button: rotate · middle/right button or Shift: pan · Ctrl+wheel (or click, then wheel): zoom · double click: reset · arrow keys: rotate · hover over a part: name, size, length · click / tap: pin · N / P: next / previous part · Esc: close
  1. 1.1 Measure your sticks and parts
    • Measure a stick with a ruler: 150 × 18 × 2 mm, with a 10 mm rounded section at each end (verified 2026-09-20); that leaves a 130 mm flat section in the middle.
    • Check with calipers: the thread of the banana jack body (≈ 8 mm; since B60 a SINGLE model on the panel, large clear); how far the jacks reach into the wall (2026-09-21): 15 mm. USB-C plug body (≈ 12 × 6.5), toggle thread (6). If it does not match, use the number you measured, not the hole table: hole = measured thread + 0.5 mm, round to the nearest drill bit, enlarge while testing. The diameters in the table are nominal; what counts is that the part goes in up to the nut.
    • The board sizes WERE MEASURED (2026-09-23), no need to measure again: board A 115 × 115 (cut to this size in Step 1.3), board B factory 50 × 50 (not cut), devkit 27.5 × 63. The plan was generated with these numbers. The only thing to check: the length of the yellow wire B:O16 → A:C11. In the box (board B at 270°) the two solder points are 145 mm apart in a straight line, ~189 mm from the edges: the wire must be 220 mm. If you cut it shorter in the layout: splice on a wire of the same gauge, solder, cover with heat-shrink (~1.7 V, harmless) — do not twist it to GND, there is no GND on B.
    • What to do if a number does not match: up to ±2 mm, nothing — Step 4.4 already says "measure, cut the rest", and the inner layer / post / rail lengths come from your real measurement there. For anything bigger, change the number in one place: fix the relevant field in uretim/kutu_veri.py, run python kutu.py — the cut list, hole tables, drawings and 3D scene are regenerated; if anything is left inconsistent the audit turns red.

    Check

    • Are the sticks straight, any cracks? Set the warped ones aside for the lid.

    • The stick has two rounded ends: every piece that needs a square joint is cut from the flat section in the middle (130 mm). Inner layer and post pieces come from a whole stick (one rounded end stays on the piece): 90 mm long, rounded end down (hidden at the base). The wall is 5 rows = 90 mm; cutting a stick in half does NOT give this length (75 mm left), so a whole stick is used for each vertical piece and the leftover flat part goes to other pieces.
    • Measure-cut-measure: cut only the base, rails and outer layer pieces now. Inner layer, posts, lid and spacers are cut to the real size once the walls are done (4.4).
    • Utility knife or fine saw; mark with a pencil before cutting. Sort the pieces into groups.

  3. 1.3 Bring board A to {kart_a_en:.0f} × {kart_a_boy:.0f} mm
    • Your board was cut to 130 × 120 mm; the plan wants 115 × 115. The excess is ~15 mm on the right, ~5 mm at the front (corner A1 stays at the back left, you do not touch the soldered area).
    • Why it is a must: uncut, the board reaches x 143 on the right and runs over the ESP32 (x 139). It does not fit in the box.
    • How: score the cut line deeply on both faces with a utility knife through the middle of the hole row (5–6 passes), then snap it over the edge of the table starting from the short side. Clean up with sandpaper. Mask / damp cloth for the glass-fibre dust.
    • Before cutting, check by eye that the cut line does not cross a soldered trace or part — the layout plan left 2×2 holes empty at the edge.

    Check

    • Board 115 × 115 mm (±1).
    • No lifted copper or broken traces on the cut edge (hold it up to the light).
    • With the board in the back-left corner of the plan (x 13, y 12) there are 27 mm left to the front wall — this space is for the 15 mm bodies of the front panel jacks and the cable bends.

    Going into the boxRuleIn stock
    J1V input banana jack pair (panel): red = V input, black = COM (board GND).CON028 · Soketler 1 Kutusu
    J2HV input banana jack (panel): SEPARATE, marked, and the ONLY YELLOW jack on the box (B60); its COM is shared with J1's COM.CON030 · Soketler 1 Kutusu
    J3LOAD banana jack pair (large, green ×2, panel): J3.1 → load negative, J3.2 → source negative. A short heavy cable from the inner end of the jacks to the barrier terminal block (HB950) next to the shunt — on the jack side a solder lug or an untinned loop between two nuts, on the barrier side an untinned twisted end (solder creeps under a screw and loosens; ring lugs are not in stock and not needed); the current follows the path J3.1 → shunt → J3.2.CON031 · Soketler 1 Kutusu
    J4Scope input banana jack (panel); COM shared.CON028 · Soketler 1 Kutusu
    J7BATTERY banana jack pair (large, blue ×2, panel): J7.1 → load resistor, J7.2 → battery negative; SEPARATE from J3 — mix them up and the cut-off does not work.CON029 · Soketler 1 Kutusu
    • Fit the eight jacks into the holes, tighten the nuts from inside. All the SAME model (large clear, B60). Colours: LOAD green ×2, BATTERY blue ×2, V/SCOPE red, COM black, HV yellow — the only yellow jack on the box, do not mix up its position.
    • After tightening the nut, slide heat-shrink over the inner end of the HV jack but DO NOT SHRINK it — the HV wire is connected in 9.3 (method ① or ② below); that is when you pull the heat-shrink over the joint and shrink it.
    • How to connect a cable to a jack (to the metal stud at the back of the jack; the same for all jacks). Do not use the nut that holds the jack to the panel for the cable — every time you tighten it the jack turns too. ① If the pack has a solder lug (a thin washer with a hole and a tab): nut → lug → second nut; solder the cable to the lug, slide heat-shrink over it — the best option. ② Without a lug: strip the cable ~18 mm, twist the strands tightly and do not tin them; make a loop with round-nose pliers and wrap it around the stud between two nuts clockwise (the loop closes as you tighten the nut), tighten the outer nut firmly. No stray strands; cover the bare part outside the nut with heat-shrink. ③ If the stud has only one nut, that nut holds the jack: you need a second nut — the M3 nut from stock (MEK034) if the stud is M3, otherwise a nut that fits the stud from a hardware store. Why untinned: under pressure solder slowly creeps and the nut loosens; on a 9.5 A path a loose joint heats up. Ring lugs are not in stock and not needed; if you want to buy some, crimp and solder the barrel of an uninsulated lug (the solder stays in the barrel, it does not go under the nut). Tighten the nuts once more the next day.
    • Prepare the heavy leads NOW (while the box is empty): connect a ≥1.5 mm² pigtail to the inner end of the four large jacks (method above; judge the gauge by stripping and measuring: bare conductor ≥ 1.4 mm for solid wire, ~1.6 mm for a stranded bundle) and label its end. Lengths (measured going around board A, 3–4 cm slack included):
      • LOAD 1 → to pole 1 of the barrier in 8.1 — 20 cm
      • LOAD 2 → to pole 2 of the barrier in 8.1 — 20 cm
      • BATTERY 1 → to Q1's drain in 8.1 — 30 cm (the longest run)
      • BATTERY 2 → to pole 2 of the barrier in 8.1 — 25 cm
      Why now: in 8.1 board A will be fitted and there is only 12 mm of blind space behind these jacks; a soldering iron does not get in there. Bend the pigtails towards the middle of the box, in 8.1 you only screw down their ends.
    • Stick on the labels of the jacks you fitted in this step right away — V · COM · HV ⚡ · LOAD 1 · LOAD 2 · SCOPE · BATTERY 1 · BATTERY 2; the remaining labels in 14.1.

    • Read the positions from the drawing and the hole table below, not from the text. The logic of the arrangement (B59): top left ON/OFF + POWER lamp, middle row COM · V · HV (the measuring probe next to COM), top right CAL · SCOPE (short patch lead), bottom row the BATTERY pair on the left, the LOAD pair on the right. All on a 18 mm grid, in the middle of stick rows 1, 3 and 5.
    • ⚠ Slide heat-shrink over the inner end of the CAL jack (solder lug or stud). Its nearest neighbour on the panel is 22 mm away; its neighbours are V and SCOPE, which can carry up to 64 V, and the back of the panel is crowded. Without heat-shrink, wrap it in insulating tape.
    • POWER lamp (LED1): push the 5 mm green LED from outside in into the Ø5 hole in the top row of the front wall (tight fit; if loose, a drop of hot glue inside the hole). ⚠ Mark the leg orientation now: long leg = positive (anode), the flat on the side of the body is on the short leg's (cathode) side. Once the LED is fitted you can no longer see which leg is longer — bend the short leg or slide heat-shrink over it. Wiring in 10.4: long leg through 10 kΩ to the +12 rail, short leg to board GND.
    • Nothing goes on the back wall in this step: the CHARGE and USB slots stay empty (the Type-C plugs go straight into the modules' sockets), the ventilation holes are open.

  18. 6.0 Fit the charging module (TP1) BEFORE board A
    Going into the boxRuleIn stock
    TP1TP4056 protected (DW01+FS8205): B± to the pack (two cells in parallel), OUT± to the load. Rprog factory 1.2 kΩ (1 A, ~0.5 A per cell). Do not charge under load: BATTERY OFF.MOD002 · Sensörler Kutusu
    • Why now: the TP4056 goes under the empty back strip of board A (9 mm to the board's underside). Once the board is in, the 27 mm module cannot be lowered and laid flat through the 12 mm gap between wall and board, and a soldering iron cannot reach its end pads.
    • Solder it at the bench first: ~20 cm of 0.5 mm² wire to the module's B+, B−, OUT+, OUT− pads (positives red, negatives black), label the ends: B+ / B− / OUT+ / OUT−. IN+/IN− stay empty (charging comes from the Type-C). The ends are connected to the fuses and the BATTERY switch in 10.3.
    • Shelf — four stick pieces (all 18 mm wide, cut across): bottom layer two 9 mm, top layer one 27 mm, stop one 5 mm. Place the two bottom pieces with a 9 mm channel between them, glue the top layer on both with CA glue. Glue the stop to the end of the top layer away from the wall, upright on its long edge (the module will rest against this edge).
    • Which oval: the one on the left seen from the front (the jack side) — in 3.2 you wrote CHARGE on its inside face; the other one (USB) is the ESP32's. Mix them up and the ESP32 ends up under board A and the board does not sit down.

    • Secure the module (TP1) with a cable tie: pass a cable tie through the channel; put the module on the shelf, the Type-C socket into the slot, the far edge against the stop (the stop takes the pushing force when you plug in, not the tie). Run the tie over the middle of the module (~13 mm from the socket), over the IC, and tighten — it must not cover the LEDs or the end pads. The module has no mounting hole — NO screws/bolts.
    • Bring the ends of the four wires up through the gap between the wall and board A, hold them to the wall temporarily with masking tape — so they are not crushed when board A goes in.

  19. 6.1 Align the feet with the board, embedded nuts
    • The layout plan left 2×2 holes empty in each board's corner: drill Ø3.2 in the middle of these four holes (four corners on A, two diagonal corners on B).
    • The board's position is in the table (wired edge to the front). The foot block overhangs the board's edge by ~6 mm, that is normal.
    • Foot block: 9 stick pieces stacked = 18 mm (this height was MEASURED for the jumper wires under the board). Layer 1 Ø3.2 (the screw goes in), layers 2 and 3 Ø6.5 = nut pocket (4 mm deep: an M3 nut is 2.4 mm, fully embedded and the laminate stays flat), layer 4 Ø3.2 — the screw tip comes out there, the layers below are not drilled, they only add height; the screw does not bottom out on wood. Why the pocket is Ø6.5: an M3 nut is 6.35 mm across the corners, it does not fit anything narrower.
    • When putting the nut into the pocket, a drop of CA glue on its outer face (CA on the nut's OUTER face — not on its thread) — the pocket is round, so on its own it does not stop the nut from turning; a turning nut neither tightens nor releases the screw. The nut stays in the box for good, that is fine: what needs to come off is the board, not the nut.
    • How the holes line up (order matters): ① Stack the top 4 layers, clamp them with a peg/tape, drill all of them at once Ø3.2 — that way the four holes come out coaxial, no marking by hand. ② Draw an alignment line on the side with a pencil (so the layers go back in the same order and the same way round). ③ Separate the layers; enlarge the hole in layers 2 and 3 to Ø6.5 (the Ø3.2 pilot centres the drill), bring layer 4 to Ø3.2. ④ First glue layers 4 + 3 + 2 with CA glue — the pocket is now a well open at the top. ⑤ Drop the nut into the well (a 6.35 mm nut centres itself in a Ø6.5 well), a drop of CA glue on its outer face, put layer 1 on top following the line and press. ⑥ Before the CA cures, screw an M3 screw in and out: if it does not go in, the layers have shifted, fix it at once. ⑦ Glue the remaining lower layers (riser, no holes) under this head.
    • Gluing to the base — with the blocks screwed to the board: screw the blocks to the board with M3 screws, put the board with its blocks in the place from the table, run a hot-glue fillet along the edges of the blocks that stick out beyond the board; once the glue has cooled, take the screws out and lift the board. The screws give the alignment: if you mark with a pen and glue them one by one, a 0.5–1 mm shift stops the screw from reaching the nut. For board B, two blocks the same way but 4 layers (8 mm) — there are no wires under B, it stays low.

  21. 6.3 ESP32, board B and spacers
    • ESP32 — in the cradle; align first, then glue. Devkit pins up, socket end ~2 mm from the back wall. Which oval: the one on the right seen from the front (the jack side) — it says USB on its inside face; the other one holds the charging module you fitted in 6.0. From outside, plug a Type-C cable through that oval into the devkit's socket marked COM and leave it plugged in: the cable sets the devkit's position, you glue the parts below against it. If the plug does not go in, slide the devkit sideways until it does — seen from the front there is 6 mm of room to the right, only 1 mm to the left (on the left is board A's back-right foot); if you need more, leave the devkit in place and file the oval out towards the COM socket.
    • Spacer four pieces: two rows, each split in the middle; the 9 mm channel between them is where the cable tie runs. The channel must line up with pins that have NO dupont connector on either side: the tie is 3.6 mm, the pins are ~1.9 mm apart — the tie cannot pass between pins, it passes over the tops of EMPTY pins. Pins in use: 3V3, 5V, GND, GPIO4, GPIO5, GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8, GPIO9, GPIO10. Look at the pin labels on the devkit, find a row of 3–4 empty pins on both sides; if the channel is not there, shift the piece lengths (back + 9 + front = 63 mm). Hot-glue the spacer to the base where the table says (±2 mm tolerance; leave room under the rails).
    • Cradle — everything CA-glued on top of the spacer, with the devkit in place and the cable plugged into COM (wrap a layer of paper around the devkit's edge: it gives 0.25 mm of play and keeps the CA glue away from the devkit): ① Side rails — 5 mm strips cut across, upright on their long edge; two on each long side, no rail where the channel is (the tie comes out there). ② Shoulder blocks — split one strip in two (9 + 9 mm); at the antenna end, rest them against the board's shoulders on either side of the antenna tab. Leave at least 22 mm between them: the tab is ~19 mm and in the middle — the blocks DO NOT TOUCH THE ANTENNA, the board's shoulders take the pushing force when plugging in the USB. The back wall holds the back end (when pulling, the devkit moves back 2 mm at most).
    • Once the CA has cured, unplug the cable and pass the cable tie through the channel: under the devkit, over the tops of the empty pins on both sides, locked on top. Tight enough that the devkit does not move, without bending the board; the tie must not press on a dupont connector, the USB sockets or the BOOT/RESET buttons. To remove: cut the tie, pull off the wires, the devkit lifts out — the cradle stays in place, put back, the devkit drops into its own spot.
    • Coat board B before fitting it. The whole divider chain (617 → 103 V) is on this board: 4–5 thin coats of nail varnish/conformal coating on both faces. Solder the T_HV and T_N6 wires FIRST, then coat the solder points too. Details and areas not to coat: the "Insulating coating" section.
    • Screw board B onto its feet. ORIENTATION MATTERS — it can be fitted four ways: the board's A1 corner (front-left) faces that corner of the box. In this orientation the 617 V input node stays furthest from every conductor in the box and the HV cable is the shortest (55 mm); the wrong orientation makes both worse.

  22. 6.4 Solder the shunt harness at the bench
    • The box gets a 5 mΩ 9.5 A shunt (R042). Datasheet (YSR series): a single piece of manganin wire Ø1.6 mm, 5 mΩ ±5%, 10 A, 10 ± 0.5 mm between legs, below the crimp (bead) on the legs only 3.5 mm of leg. DO NOT USE the other 5 mΩ in the same box (R043, no current rating printed): its datasheet is a generic catalogue and the alloy is unknown (it may be copper-nickel, ±400 ppm/°C) — at 9.5 A the shunt heats up ~40 °C, and the reading drifts ~1.6% with copper-nickel, ~0.1% with manganin. The 15 mΩ (R044) stays at 3.4 A but reads 3 times finer — the spare for mA work; it is swapped with the terminal screws. The heavy load cables are NOT SOLDERED to the legs: the legs go into the two poles of the XP128 10 mm terminal block (CON064) — the spacing is already 10 mm, try it before bending, bend slightly if it does not fit; the heavy cables do not fit the XP128 either, they join at the barrier terminal block (HB950) and a single bridge goes to each XP128 pole (7.1, 8.1). Mark which shunt leg is RS.1 (LOAD 1 side) and which RS.2 (LOAD 2).
    • Kelvin wires = two thin sense wires that carry no current: they read the shunt voltage without the contact resistance of the terminal block (a few mΩ — as much as the shunt itself) mixing in. Solder them to the crimp itself on the legs: the datasheet shows the measuring point there; the 3.5 mm of leg below the crimp goes into the terminal block — leave it bare, NO solder/contact at the screw. If the solder point moves 1 mm, the shunt's apparent value changes ~4%; the calibration in 12.2 corrects that. Soldering: iron ≤ 350 °C, ≤ 3–4 s per joint (the datasheet limits it to 350 °C / 3.5 s); tin the wire first, use flux. DO NOT PUT hot glue on the joints — at full current the shunt heats up ~45 °C, the glue softens and stops the shunt from cooling; the cable tie in 7.2 takes the strain, heat-shrink over the joint if you like. The Kelvin pair S+ (RS.1) and S− (RS.2) twisted, the star GND to RS.2 at the same point as S−. Wires ~20 cm (in the box ~12 cm from the shunt to the front edge of board A). A 3-way female header on the end of the three wires (cut from CON018).
    • Male pins on the ends of the T_SP / T_SN / T_YILDIZ wires on board A: the harness plugs in with a connector, the board stays removable.

  23. 6.5 Q1 harness and heatsink
    • Screw Q1 to the heatsink insulated: mica/silicone insulator + bushing + thermal paste. A 1-pin female header on the gate leg, with heat-shrink.
    • Fasten the heatsink to the three-piece stick corner bracket with an M3 screw + nut.
    • Connect the heatsink to board GND through 1 MΩ (R026): one end of the resistor under the heatsink's screw nut, the other end to board GND (A:T_YILDIZ or the shunt's RS.2 leg; ⚠ NOT the black end of the 24 V terminal block — that is the −12 rail). Why a resistor: the mica insulates the heatsink, so it stays a floating metal plate in the closed box; the resistor drains static build-up and defines its potential. Why NOT a direct wire: if the mica is ever punctured, the heatsink is connected to Q1's drain, i.e. BATTERY 1 (38 V in the battery test) — a plain wire would short that to GND, and there is no fuse of ours on that path. With 1 MΩ, 38 µA flows at worst.

  25. 7.1 Connect the load path
    • Power node barrier terminal block (HB950, CON011) next to the shunt block: run a short heavy bridge from each XP128 pole to the matching barrier pole. Nothing but the shunt leg + that single bridge goes into the XP128.
    • The heavy cable of the LOAD 1 jack (≥1.5 mm², fitted in 5.2) → barrier pole 1 (= RS.1 node); barrier pole 2 (= RS.2 node) → the heavy cable of the LOAD 2 jack. On the barrier side: strip the wire ~10 mm, twist it tightly, do not tin it, lay it clockwise under the screw (and its washer, if any) and tighten — a tinned end loosens under a screw over time (reason in 5.2). ⚠ Ring lugs are NOT in stock and not needed; if you want to buy some, a lug with its barrel soldered as in 5.2.
    • Keep it short: all the measured current flows through this path (continuous ≤ 9.5 A, the thermal limit of the 5 mΩ shunt; 3.4 A if the 15 mΩ is fitted). The XP128 terminal block holding the shunt is 10 A: do not exceed it, not even briefly.
    • Check the print on top of the HB950 (e.g. "300V 15A"): it must be at least 10 A. If it says less, take that number as the box's current limit and write it on the panel under the LOAD label.

  27. 8.1 Connect Q1 to the load path
    • The power node is at the barrier, not at the XP128. Glue/screw an HB950 2-pin barrier terminal block (CON011) next to the shunt block. Only the shunt leg + a single bridge wire stay in each XP128 pole; all the heavy cables join at the barrier. Reason: if a Ø1.6 mm manganin rod and a stranded cable go into the XP128's cage together, the rod takes the pressure and the cable works loose — on a 10 A path a loose terminal heats up. No effect on the measurement: the Kelvin ends are on the shunt's leg, not at this node; contact resistance at the node does not change the current and does not enter the measured voltage.
    • Barrier pole 1 (= RS.1 node): LOAD 1 jack · Q1's source · the bridge to XP128 pole 1.
    • Barrier pole 2 (= RS.2 node): LOAD 2 jack · BATTERY 2 jack · the bridge to XP128 pole 2.
    • BATTERY 1 jack → Q1's drain (does not pass the barrier, a single cable).
    • All heavy cable; the jack ends were connected in 5.2. On the barrier side, twisted untinned ends under the screw (and its washer, if any) — two or three ends fit in one pole, lay them all the same way (clockwise). A tinned end loosens under a screw over time (5.2). Ring lugs are not in stock and not needed.
    • When changing the shunt (5 mΩ ↔ 15 mΩ) only the two XP128 screws are loosened — the heavy cables and the Kelvin joints stay in place.

  31. 9.3 HV jack and cable anchor
    • Prerequisite: side B of Layout 5.12 must be finished (HV soldered to B:D8, yellow wire B:O16 → A:C11).
    • HV jack → board B D8: silicone probe cable (KBL004). By a short route, not running parallel to other wires.
    • The cable's voltage class — decide here, do not ask: read the print on the jacket (614 V full scale). ① If it says 614 V or more (e.g. 1 kV / 20 kV silicone probe cable): use it as is. ② If it says less, or there is no print at all: cover the cable with heat-shrink along its full length (a second insulation; the heat-shrink overlapping 10 mm at the ends) and write the value you read on the panel under the HV label — do not measure above that value. The jacket of an unprinted cable alone does not count as 614 V; covered, the second layer carries the risk, and the box itself is an insulator anyway. ③ Either way the cable must be one piece: no splices / screw connectors.
    • Anchor: glue three stick pieces on top of each other and glue them upright to the base in front of board B (the planned place); hold the HV cable to it with a cable tie — when the cable is pulled, the tie resists, not the D8 joint.
    • HV's return is also the COM jack; no separate wire.

  32. 10.1 Set MT1 to 5.0 V and MT2 to 24.0 V with no load
    • Set the two MT3608s at the bench with no load connected: watch the output with a multimeter, turn the trimpot anticlockwise. The factory setting can go up to 28 V: do not connect an unadjusted module to the ESP32 or the board (28 V kills the ESP32).
    • MT1 → 5.0 V: a 18650 on the input (3.0–4.2 V). MT2 → 24.0 V: feed 5 V to the input — in the box it is fed from the B0505S's isolated 5 V; at the bench a USB charger or the MT1 output you just set is enough.
    • Label both: MT1 (5 V), MT2 (24 V).
    • Try the B0505S at the bench too (before it goes on the wall). The body has no pin names: with the printed face towards you and the pins down, the leftmost pin under the dot is 1. Hi-Link datasheet: 1 = +Vin, 2 = −Vin, 4 = −Vout, 6 = +Vout (no 3 and 5) — the two pins side by side are the INPUT, the two spaced apart are the OUTPUT. ⚠ On the Mornsun B0505S 1 = GND, 2 = Vin: do not go by another brand's diagram; feeding the input reversed damages the module (−0.7 V limit). Do not clip alligator clips onto the pins (2.5 mm between 1–2): first solder thin wire to all four pins (iron ≤ 300 °C, ≥ 1.5 mm from the body), cover with heat-shrink — that is how the module is fitted in 10.2 anyway. The body must say 2WR3 (the 1 W version is not enough at power-up, B58f). 5 V on its input (USB charger or the adjusted MT1), read 5–7 V on its output (with no load an unregulated module reads a little high; in the box MT2 loads it). The datasheet does not recommend running it unloaded for long: read and switch off.

    • MT2 output 23.8–24.2 V (input at 4.5–5.5 V).
    • B0505S: output (6 ↔ 4) 5–7 V (no load); unpowered, pin 2 (−Vin) ↔ pin 4 (−Vout) does not beep.

    • Back wall (from inside): two 18650 holders one above the other — YUVA1 below, YUVA2 above (position in the table). Hot-glue them — no bolts (user decision): first mark the position with a pencil (hot glue only gives you a few seconds to adjust), run two beads along the full length of the holder's base, press against the wall 10 s. Where it lands between the inner layer sticks, leave the glue thick — it fills the 2 mm gap. Orientation: the end of YUVA1 where its red wire comes out to the LEFT (towards F1P), YUVA2's to the RIGHT (towards F2). DO NOT insert the cells yet (10.5). The top of YUVA2 is 6 mm from the lid.
    • The charging module (TP1) was fitted in 6.0, before board A; do not touch it here.
    • At the bench first: solder the wires to MT1 and MT2 (like TP1; in the box the iron does not reach the pads easily): push the wire in from the component side of the board, solder underneath, trim the excess — the back of the module must sit flat on the wall. Label the ends. Which wire goes to which pad and the cut lengths are in the cable table and drawing of 10.3 / 10.4 (numbered). Write '−12 side' on MT2's IN− end.
    • Fuse holder = two separate clips (FUS009), not a single body: solder the two clips onto a strip of at most 25 mm cut from the perfboard left over from board A — first put the fuse into both clips, pass the legs through the strip, solder; the fuse spacing comes out right by itself. Join the two legs of each clip underneath; push the wire in from the front through the empty hole next to the clip and solder it to the clip leg at the back. Three strips: F0, F1P, F2. (A covered KF-03 was tried: at 27 × 14 mm it does not fit the layout — F1P goes under board A and the covers overlap.)
    • Fixing — hot glue (user decision 2026-09-30): MT1, MT2, B0505S, 680 µF, KL and the three fuse strips are hot-glued to the wall; to remove, drip isopropyl alcohol and lift with a plastic card. Glue on the BACK or the edge of the PCB — not on the chip and the inductor (the parts that get hot). The MT1/MT2 trimpots face in and stay reachable. The boards, ESP32, shunt and Q1 are not glued.
    • MT1 and MT2 on the left of the back wall, one above the other (x 43–79; MT1 z 24, MT2 z 47). MT1's OUT pads to the LEFT (F0 and B0505S), MT2's IN pads to the LEFT (B0505S and 680 µF).
    • B0505S (IZ) to the left of MT2, pins down, glued by its body. ⚠ This module is the ONLY part separating the box's two grounds: the input side (1 +Vin, 2 −Vin) and the output side (4 −Vout, 6 +Vout) must not be joined by any wire.
    • MT2's input capacitor (CB, 680 µF 16 V, C042) above MT2, lying down. Solder its legs to MT2's input pads: long leg IN+, ⚠ striped leg NEGATIVE → IN−.
    • 24 V internal terminal block (KL, CON007) above the B0505S; screws facing in. Write with a pen which screw is +: in 10.4 MT2's output and the board's 24 V wires are screwed in here with the same polarity.
    • Analog fuse F0 below the B0505S, to the left of MT1 (position in the table); it takes a 1 A fast glass fuse (FUS003) — DO NOT FIT it for now, in 10.5 it stays out for the first power-up sequence.
    • Cell fuses F1P and F2 on the bottom row (position in the table); they take 2 A F glass fuses (FUS004). Why the rating is so high: the fuse is on the cell's positive, so the charging current flows through it too (1.00 A; all of it if only one cell is fitted) — a smaller one blows on the first charge.

  34. 10.3 Wire the battery pack (two cells in parallel)
    • The four ends of TP1 you soldered in 6.0 (B+, B−, OUT+, OUT−) come up through the gap between the wall and board A; remove the tape and connect the ends as in the table below.
    • Following the table below; with the cells NOT INSERTED. The two cells in parallel: each cell's positive goes through ITS OWN fuse (F1P, F2) and they join at the TP4056's B+, the negatives at B−. H1+ / H2+ DO NOT GO straight to B+. Why: the TP4056's protection FET (FS8205) is between B− and OUT−; a short at the cell ends or in the cell wires stays OUTSIDE that FET, the DW01A cannot interrupt it. And in parallel there is one more thing: if one cell shorts internally, the other tries to fill it with no fuse in between.
    • The cell wires are the holder's own wires: the red one (+, the end without the spring) straight to the fuse clip, the black one to TP4056 B−. F2's output runs along the back wall to F1P's output clip; a single wire goes from there to TP4056 B+ (the two cells are in parallel here). If a holder wire is shorter than the length in the table, splice it (solder + heat-shrink).
    • On the TP4056 the pack goes to B±, the load to OUT±. The largest current is 1.00 A while charging (half to each cell); 0.5 mm² carries that easily, no heavy wire needed.
    • BATTERY switch (SWP1) on the pack side: TP1.OUT+ → BATTERY → MT1 input. When off, MT1 draws nothing; this is the box's only switch. The KTS102's middle pin to TP4056 OUT+; the other wire to the outer pin that beeps with the middle one when the switch is in the ON position (find it with a multimeter).
    • MT1's 5 V output to the ESP32: the devkit has a single 5V pin and in 11.1 the 5V wire of the J5 cable also goes there — make a Y-splice: cut a single-pin piece off a female header (CON018), solder BOTH MT1's 5 V wire and the J5 cable's 5V wire to its tail, cover with heat-shrink; this single female end goes onto the devkit's 5V pin (a male header does not fit a male pin). For GND, the devkit's second GND pin.
    • ⚠ At first insertion the two cells must be at the same voltage (±0.1 V): otherwise the higher one fills the lower one with a large current. Measure both separately before inserting; if the difference is large, first insert only one and charge it fully as in 10.6 (4.2 V), take it out, insert the other one and charge it, then insert both together.

  35. 10.4 Wire the analog supply: 5 V → F0 → B0505S → MT2 → terminal block → board
    Going into the boxRuleIn stock
    J624 V input. At the bench: XT30 (CON058) — MALE end on the board side (with pins), FEMALE end on the power-supply side; the side carrying voltage should have the shrouded socket. Insulated wire, red = +, black = −. In the box (B58): the XT30 is cut off, the wires go to the internal terminal block (KL) — the 24 V comes from the box's own battery (MT2), no external supply.
    • The wires of the board's 24 V input (J6: C34 red, C36 black) are screwed into the terminal block — the board comes out without desoldering. If the wire ends still have the XT30 male from the bench, cut it off: no external supply, the XT30 is not used.
    • Following the table below: 5 V bus (MT1 output) → F0 (1 A fast, FUS003, inside the box, 10.2) → B0505S pin 1 (+Vin); pin 2 (−Vin) → the negative of the 5 V bus. B0505S pin 6 (+Vout) → MT2 IN+, pin 4 (−Vout) → MT2 IN−; MT2 output → terminal block (+ → C34, − → C36).
    • CB (680 µF) on MT2's input terminals, at the same point as the B0505S wires: long leg → IN+, striped leg → IN−. Why: at power-up, while charging the board's 136 µF, MT2 draws a peak current the B0505S cannot supply; without the capacitor MT2 collapses its input and starts over, and the board may not reach 24 V (B58f simulation).
    • Rule (audited): the B0505S's output side (MT2 input, terminal −, the board's −12 rail) DOES NOT TOUCH board GND by any path. The B0505S is the only part separating the box's two grounds: a single wire joining the two sides shorts −12 to GND.
    • Why F0 is on the 5 V side: a fault in the analog chain (B0505S, MT2, board) must not be able to pull down the pack and the 5 V bus. The 24 V side needs no separate protection — the board's own F1 is there, and the B0505S's power is limited to 1–2 W and it shuts itself off on a short.
    • Fuse: F1 on the board. At power-up the board's 136 µF charges; since B58 the switch is on the 5 V side and the 24 V rises through the B0505S + MT2, so the surge is softer than from a stiff 24 V source — but the calculation assumes the worst case (stiff source): this surge blows a genuine 50 mA fast (F) fuse (the surge I²t is 3–5 times the melting value — Littelfuse 217/218 datasheets, the audit calculates it). Decision (2026-09-24): the fitted fuse stays, T goes to the later plan. Right now the holder has a '50 mA' in it and it has never blown in 20+ power-ups — good news on its own, but it does not tell you which fuse it is: a genuine 50 mA F would blow on this surge. The 0.3 Ω measured in B52 cannot be 50 mA (a 50 mA wire reads 15–21 Ω) — 0.3 Ω is the 400 mA class. Together they say one thing: ignore the label in the holder, trust the ohmmeter. If you are curious, take the fuse out and measure its cold resistance: 15–21 Ω → really 50 mA (then it is a T type, since it did not blow); around 0.3 Ω → 400 mA class (FUS001). Either way there is short-circuit protection and the build does not wait on it. If a T (time-delay) 50 mA glass fuse (Littelfuse 218.050 / ESKA / Schurter, margin ≥ 10×) is bought later, it is fitted and switched on and off 20 times: +12/−12 must come up every time. The FUS010 in stock is an F type, and a 315 mA F gives no margin on the surge either — neither is worth swapping in. No fuse opens on a partial TL072 failure.
    • POWER lamp: solder the 10 kΩ resistor (R060) to the LED's long leg, cover with heat-shrink; the resistor's other end to the POSITIVE screw of the terminal block (KL.+ = +12 rail). The LED's short leg (cathode) to the solder lug of the COM jack (= board GND; cable 24 in the table, 10 cm). ⚠ Do not connect it to MT1's negative: that point only joins board GND through J5 in 11.1, in 10.5 the lamp would not light. ⚠ Do not connect it to the NEGATIVE screw of the terminal block either: that is the −12 rail, 7912 cannot source current in that direction, the rail drifts.

The audit builds the node graph from this list and checks that the board's −12 rail stays separate from board GND — the two sides are separated only inside the B0505S.

    Check

    • B0505S pin 2 (−Vin) ↔ pin 4 (−Vout): should not beep (isolation intact).
    • Terminal − (C36) ↔ board GND (C29): should not beep.
    • Polarity (BEFORE power): terminal + ↔ MT2 OUT+ and the board's C34 should beep; terminal − ↔ MT2 OUT− and C36 should beep. If reversed, both TL072s die at the first power-up (the XT30 was keyed, the terminal block is not).
    • With F0 fitted, the 5 V bus ↔ B0505S Vin is connected; with F0 removed, open (the fuse really is in the path).
    • CB polarity (BEFORE power): the capacitor's striped leg ↔ MT2 IN− should beep; an electrolytic fitted backwards heats up and bursts at the first power-up.
  36. 10.5 First power-up in the box — from the battery
    • The socketed ICs are not fitted (they go in during 11.1), the J5 cable is not connected, BATTERY OFF, no USB plugged in, NO fuse in the F0 holder (the measurement side stays off at first).
    • Insert the cells (mind the polarity; the ±0.1 V rule is in 10.3). BATTERY ON: 4.95–5.05 V on the 5 V bus, the ESP32 starts. A clone devkit may have no VBUS diode: read 0 V on the VBUS pin of the USB socket. If you read 5 V, MT1 is back-feeding the USB → put the Schottky SR5100 from stock (D004; striped end to the ESP32) in the 5 V wire going to the ESP32, cover it with heat-shrink and raise MT1 to 5.3 V (~0.4 V drops across the diode).
    • Switch BATTERY off, fit F0 (1 A), switch BATTERY back on: 24.0 V at the terminal block, +12 V / −12 V on the board (V35 / R33, GND: V36); the POWER lamp lights.
    • If the box does not power up (with BATTERY on the ESP32 does not start at all or flashes once, the POWER lamp does not light): the pack protection (DW01A) has tripped on the inrush current. Switch BATTERY off, wait 2 seconds, switch it on again. If it persists, charge the battery as in 10.6 and try — in the simulation all four behaviour models of the B0505S start up with a full battery. If it does not start with a full battery either: switch BATTERY off, solder the 3 × 1 Ω 1 W resistor (R052) in series between the B0505S's +Vo wire and MT2's IN+ terminal, cover with heat-shrink, try. If it still fails, replace the TP4056 module with the spare from stock (MOD002, as in 6.0). If 24 V does not come up (the ESP32 is on but there is no 24 V at the terminal block, or the POWER lamp blinks): if the series resistor is fitted, remove it — this B0505S is the type that shuts down on overload and retries, the resistor is too much for it; if it is not fitted, check that both legs of CB are soldered to MT2's input and its polarity.
    • Look at the −12 rail with the scope (MT3608 + B0505S ripple): if you see more than 50 mV, add 68 µF 50 V (C035) + 100 nF (C008) at MT2's output (the noise concern of 5.12.23 is measured here). ⚠ Most of the 100 µF capacitors in stock are 16 V — DO NOT FIT them on the 24 V rail, they burst.
    • 🛑 Switch BATTERY OFF after measuring. The next step (11.1) fits the ICs into their sockets, the ADS module and the 10-wire J5 cable — these are not plugged into a powered board: a badly seated IC or a module plugged in backwards dies instantly.

    Check

    • +12 V: +11.5 … +12.5 V. −12 V: −11 … −13 V.
    • Voltage between the −12 rail ↔ board GND ≈ −12 V (if you read 0 V, the two sides of the B0505S are joined somewhere — switch off at once).
    • After 10 min, MT1, B0505S, MT2 and 7912 are warm, not hot.
  37. 10.6 Charging rule and label
    • Charging: switch the BATTERY switch OFF, then plug a single Type-C into the CHARGE slot — both cells charge together (1.00 A, half per cell). Do not charge with BATTERY on: under load the TP4056 cannot finish charging.
    • ⚠ While charging, the box's ground (COM) is connected to the charger's ground: do not measure while charging, never on HV.
    • Label (on the back panel, next to the CHARGE slot): "CHARGE: battery switch off · no measuring while charging".

    Check

    • The TP4056's LED is red while charging and blue when done (seen from the back edge of board A with the lid open). With the lid closed the light only leaks dimly around the edge of the slot — if you cannot see it, wait ≈ 3.6 hours.
    • Unplug the USB, BATTERY ON: the ESP32 starts, the WiFi panel comes up, the POWER lamp lights — the box is completely wireless.
  38. 11.1 J5 cable and ICs
    • BATTERY OFF (you switched it off in 10.5). Fit the ICs into the sockets: U3, U4 (LM358), U5, U8 (TL072). Mind the notch.
    • Plug the ADS modules into their sockets.
    • Plug the 10-wire cable onto header J5 (mapping in Layout 1.12). Do not mix up 3V3 and 5V.
    • CAL jack: a single female jumper on the devkit's GPIO10 pin, 22 kΩ (R059) in series at its end, soldered to the inner end of the jack; carefully keep the jumper clear of the SCL (GPIO9) pin next to it.
    • Plug the USB into the devkit's socket marked COM, through the back slot.

  39. 11.2 Vref and I²C gates
    • Power: BATTERY ON. You can plug the USB into the PC for the serial console — with BATTERY on the battery carries the load (MT1's 5.0 V overrides the USB's ~4.7 V). Do not plug in USB with BATTERY off: the measurement side also tries to run from the PC (~0.35 A, close to the limit of a USB 2.0 port).
    • Gate 1 — Vref. Multimeter referenced to board GND: ① TL431 cathode = 2.495 V (±2% → 2.445–2.545 V). ② Pin 1 of U3 (hole A:R8) = 1.7153 V (±10 mV). ③ Repeat the same measurement with the dividers connected — if it does not shift, the buffer works. If it fails: ① wrong → TL431 orientation / 220R feed; ① right, ② wrong → U3's socket, its notch, or U3's +5 V supply (at 3.3 V the output does not rise high enough).
    • Gate 2 — I²C. In the serial console #: both 0x48 and 0x49 must appear in the list. If it fails: SDA/SCL swapped, ADDR pin floating (0x48 = GND, 0x49 = +3V3) or no pull-up. Do not go on to calibration with an address missing — the missing channel silently reads zero.
    • Do not start Step 12 until both gates have passed.
    • WiFi settings from the serial console: Ns<web password>, Na<ssid>, Np<password>; status N?.
    GATE 1 — Guide 01 Vref gate: TL431 cathode and U3A output (fit an LM358 in the U3 socket).

    GATE 2 — Guide 02: # in the firmware — both 0x48 and 0x49 must appear.

  40. 12.1 Calibration

    From the serial console (USB). Every command writes the setting to NVS. The gain calibration (i, g) rejects values below 5% of full scale — the 'minimum' column.

    CommandWhat it doesWhenMinimum
    s0.005Enter the shunt value (5 mΩ fitted)Once. When changing to 15 mΩ: s0.015 + Z.—
    ZCurrent zeroWith nothing connected to LOAD.—

    nSwitch to the NORMAL rangeV channel ±32 V.—

  41. 12.2 Gate 3 — current (two stages)
    • Rule: the test source must be independent of the box. It CANNOT be the box's own battery pack: the pack negative is board GND, so if you draw current from it through LOAD the return current flows through the board GND wire (J5 cable) — the measurement is corrupted and the thin wire heats up. Test source: bench supply (WCT-200-24 + MOD011 buck, set to 3.7 V) → 3.3 Ω 11 W (R049) ≈ 1.1 A. The WCT is no longer connected to the box (B58): it is an isolated test source.
    • The firmware rejects a gain calibration below 5% of full scale (1638 codes): with 5 mΩ that means 2.6 A, 1.1 A is not enough. The gain correction (i) is independent of the shunt → fit the 15 mΩ (R044) first, s0.015, Z with no load; buck + 3.3 Ω in series through LOAD 1–2, multimeter on its 10 A range in series, i<measured>.
    • Then fit the 5 mΩ, s0.005, Z; measure the same ~1.1 A: it should agree with the multimeter within ±2%. For ≥2.6 A: buck 3.9 V + three 3.3 Ω in parallel (1.1 Ω, ≈3.5 A, 30 s; the MOD011 is rated 10 A) with i. Reverse the leads: the sign should change.
    • If it is not within ±2%: the shunt's apparent value is not 5 mΩ (datasheet ±5%, the position of the Kelvin joint shifts it ~4% per mm). If the board reads X A and the multimeter Y A, set the s value to 0.005 × X ÷ Y (e.g. X 1.15, Y 1.10 → s0.00523), Z, measure again. Or give i directly with the 5 mΩ fitted, using the ≥2.6 A route: then the shunt's real value goes into the gain, do not touch s.
    GATE 3 — Guide 03 Current channel: Z zero, known current, reverse current.
    off-board parts needed: J3, RS
  42. 12.3 Gate 4 — NORMAL voltage
    • n; connect the V jack to COM with a short lead (a real 0 V) and z, then remove the lead. ⚠ Do not give z with the V jack open: the input floats and the reading settles around Vref (~1.5 V); if zero is set at that point every reading shifts by that much (on the 2026-10-04 board: 1.456 V open, −0.23 V shorted). Apply a known voltage (bench supply 5–12 V — NOT the box's own battery, rule 12.2) to V–COM, compare with the multimeter, g<measured>; connect it reversed: the sign should change.
    GATE 4 — Guide 04 NORMAL: z, g<volt>, reversed input.
    off-board parts needed: J1
  43. 12.4 Gate 5 — HIGH voltage
    • y; first connect the HV jack to COM with a short lead, z, remove the lead (as in 12.3; do not zero it while open). Then 12 V (bench supply), then 24 V (the WCT's own output). Since B58 the box runs only from its own battery: the WCT is not connected to the box and can freely be the test source here. (In the old arrangement the WCT powered the box and its negative was the −12 rail — that rule is gone.)
    • The gain calibration needs ≥31 V: connect two isolated supplies in series (if you have them) or leave the HV gain at the factory 1.0 (divider 1% metal film, error ≤ 1%). One-hand rule.
    GATE 5 — Guide 05 HIGH: 12 V first, then in steps. One hand, hands clear.
    off-board parts needed: J2
  44. 12.5 Gate 6 — oscilloscope
    • Signal source: the board's CAL output — switch it on with X<hz> in the serial console, off with x; on the panel a short lead CAL jack → SCOPE jack (COM is already common). Capture with the t commands; a square wave and its frequency should appear. The amplitude shows as ≈2.7 V, NOT 3.3 V: CAL's 22 kΩ series resistor and the scope input's ~103 kΩ (R20 100 kΩ + R23 2.7 kΩ) form a divider, 103/125 ≈ 82% (the old '1 kΩ series, ≤ 1%' note went out of date when B55g moved to 22 kΩ).
    GATE 6 — Guide 06 Oscilloscope: known square wave, ta.
    off-board parts needed: J4
  45. 12.6 Gate 7 — fast current path
    • Resistive load (bench supply + 3.3 Ω, rule 12.2) through LOAD; w → PF ≈ 1.
    GATE 7 — Guide 07 Fast current path: w on a resistive load → PF ≈ 1.
    off-board parts needed: —
  46. 12.7 Gate 8 — battery test
    • Failsafe: with BATTERY off and during RESET, Q1's gate is 0 V (BATTERY 1 ↔ BATTERY 2 should not beep).
    • Instead of a battery, a bench supply (buck 4.0 V; the cells in the box are part of the pack, do not take them out) + 3.3 Ω 11 W, with BATTERY 1 – BATTERY 2 and the V jack (USE: battery capacity): P3.5, p1 → ≈1.2 A should flow. Slowly lower the buck to 3.4 V: the board must stop the test (current 0, Q1 gate 0 V). This way you test the cut-off threshold more precisely than with a real battery.
    GATE 8 — Battery test: Q1's gate must stay off with the board off and during RESET (the failsafe item in the bench list).
    off-board parts needed: J7, Q1, RS
  47. 13.1 Make the lid
    • Lay out the lid rows like the base (joints staggered), glue the two rails underneath between the posts. The rails with their 18 mm face upright (hanging down). ⚠ DO NOT PUT the rails against the side wall — set each one 0.5 mm in (1.0 mm of fit clearance in total). If you put them against the wall, the lid assembly is exactly as wide as the opening and does not go in; stick tolerance and the wood moving with humidity eat up this clearance. If you put a business card in between while laying the lid upside down on a flat surface, the clearance comes out by itself.
    • Drill the rails: put the lid in place; behind the four Ø3.2 holes in the side wall there is the 2 mm lid rail, with no hole yet. Pass the iron tip through the outer hole and drill the rail too — the hole is the guide so they come out coaxial, no marking (the inner layer method from 5.1). Do it without lifting the lid.
    • Glue the nut blocks WITH THE LID ON THE BENCH — not inside the box. After drilling the rails, lift the lid off and put it upside down on the table (rails up). Push an M3x12 bolt into each rail hole from outside (from the face of the rail that faces the wall); on its end screw the 4-layer block with its embedded nut (layer 1 Ø3.2 · layers 2–3 Ø6.5 nut pocket · layer 4 Ø3.2) — a drop of CA glue on the nut's outer face (CA on the nut's OUTER face — not on its thread), the same as the foot block in 6.1. The block is now self-centred on the bolt: put CA glue on the contact face and press it against the inner face of the rail. Once cured, take the bolt out. You do not have to match two independent measurements; since a nut cannot be held inside with the lid closed, this block is a must (B54).
    • Do not glue the lid.

  48. 13.2 Try the lid — then TAKE IT OFF
    • Once the blocks have cured, tighten the four M3x12 bolts with washers: tighten fully once, try taking it on and off. No thread in the wood, no hand needs to go inside. (The holes were made in 4.7.)
    • Then take the bolts out and LIFT the lid off — the lid stays off until Step 14. The final tidy-up (14.1) puts cable ties inside the box: that cannot be done with the lid on.
    • In this step the lid gets finished and tried; it does not stay on the box. Closing is in Step 14.

    Check

    • With the bolts in, the lid does not come off when pulled by hand.
    • The bolts are out, the lid is off the box — the box is open again.
    • All four holes land on the rail's nut block (the bolt does not spin freely).
  49. 14.1 Label and tidy up
    • Write/stick on all the panel labels — complete list: Front panel: LOAD 1 (load −) · LOAD 2 (source −) · BATTERY 1 (resistor ← battery +) · BATTERY 2 (battery −) · V · COM (= LOAD 2 = BATTERY 2) · SCOPE · ON / OFF (BATTERY) · CAL (→ short lead to SCOPE) · POWER (±12 V present) · HV ⚡
      Back panel: CHARGE (with BATTERY off) · USB (⚡ unplug when measuring HV)
    • On the back panel, next to the CHARGE slot, the charging rule label (10.6). Next to the USB slot: ⚠ unplug the USB when HV is present.
    • Tidy the cables with cable ties; the HV cable on its own and ≥ 20 mm from the others.
    • Box principle: valuable parts (boards, ESP32, shunt, Q1) are not glued; the 18650 holders, modules (MT1, MT2, B0505S), 680 µF, KL and the fuse strips are held with hot glue. When moving to another enclosure, take out the screws and cable ties, unplug the connectors; lift the hot-glued parts by dripping isopropyl alcohol and using a plastic card.

    Check

    • Shake the box: nothing moves inside.
    • The lid is still off: no tools, wire offcuts or screws left inside.
  50. 14.2 Fit the lid and bolt it down
    • Put the lid (made in 13.1) in place; through the four holes made in 4.7, fit the M3x12 bolts with washers from outside and tighten them into the embedded nuts in the rail.
    • The box closes here: from now on there is no work inside the box. If something inside needs changing, the four bolts come out and the lid lifts off — nothing breaks, since the boards and the battery block are held with screws/cable ties.
    • Check one last time that the cells are in place (they were inserted in 10.5): the holders are under the lid, to change a cell you have to open the lid. Not needed for charging — the CHARGE slot is outside.

The board's V and I readings must be within ±1% / ±2% of the multimeter.
    • With the short CAL → SCOPE lead: a square wave shows on the panel.

    • If you want to try the battery capacity test with a real battery (optional): the two 18650 cells in the box are part of the pack, do not take them out — get a third cell.

When it is done: what do I measure from where

MeasurementWhich terminalHow to connectResolution
Voltage, ≤ ±32 VV (red) + COM (black)With alligator-clip leads, in parallel with the circuit. Range: n.1.04 mV step
Voltage, ±614 VHV (YELLOW) + COM (black)Range: y. One-hand rule. DO NOT plug the USB into the PC — use the WiFi panel (COM = board GND = USB ground). If the circuit being measured is earthed (mains-powered supply, a circuit with a PC), DO NOT USE HV: this board is for floating (battery / DC-DC) circuits.18.8 mV step
Current, ≤ 9.5 A continuousLOAD 1 – LOAD 2Current is measured on the negative line: the source's + goes directly to the load's +, it does not enter the box. Break the negative line: the load's negative to LOAD 1, the source's negative to LOAD 2. For voltage at the same time, connect only the V jack to the circuit's positive; DO NOT clip anything to COM — COM already is LOAD 2. If you clip COM to the circuit's negative (LOAD 1 side) the shunt is bypassed: the reading drops and the thin lead heats up. The limit is the heating of the 5 mΩ shunt (Ø1.6 mm manganin, manufacturer 10 A; continuous 9.5 A) and the XP128 terminal block (10 A) holding the shunt: DO NOT EXCEED 10 A, not even briefly. If you need mA resolution, fit the 15 mΩ (R044), s0.015 + Z: 3.4 A continuous, 0.52 mA step.1.56 mA step
Power and energy (W, Wh)V + COM and LOAD togetherWith voltage and current connected at the same time, the board calculates the power itself; correct for reactive loads too.signed, real power
Oscilloscope, -64 … +47 VSCOPE (red) + COMTo see the waveform. Time base 100 µs – 500 ms/div. Asymmetric range: the negative side is wider.up to 83 kSa/s
Power — the box's own batteryBATTERY ON (single switch)The box runs only from its own battery (B58: no external supply). Two 18650 in parallel: runtime ≈ 5 hours (ESP32 on WiFi, analog on). Used without USB the box floats completely: the safest state for HV measurements. Charging: BATTERY OFF, a single Type-C into the CHARGE slot — both cells charge together (≈ 3.6 hours). Do not measure while charging: the charging cable ties COM to the charger's ground. Have BATTERY ON when plugging the USB into the PC: the battery carries the load; when it is off, the measurement side also tries to run from the PC (~0.35 A).2 × 18650 in parallel
Battery capacity (mAh)BATTERY 1 – BATTERY 2 + load resistor + V jackRequired: V jack → battery + (COM already is battery −, no extra wire). Battery + → load resistor → BATTERY 1; battery − → BATTERY 2. The battery's + is never plugged directly into a BATTERY jack: two wires come off it, one to the resistor, one to V. Leave LOAD empty. Battery ≤ 31 V: n, above that y. Choosing the resistor: current = battery V ÷ R, limit 6.5 A — for a 3.7 V 18650, 3.3 Ω 11 W (1.1 A, 4 W in the resistor). P<cutoff>, p1. ⚠ DO NOT MIX UP the polarity: connected backwards, the current flows through Q1's body diode and the board CANNOT STOP it (even with the MOSFET off; ~1.1 A continuous with 3.3 Ω). If the board reports a 'reversed / bypass' error it does not start the test, but the current does not stop — unplug the lead at once.≤ 38 V battery
If the box does not power upBATTERY switchIf the box does not power up when BATTERY is switched on (the ESP32 does not start at all or flashes once, the POWER lamp does not light): the battery is low — switch BATTERY off, charge the battery (CHARGE, BATTERY off), then switch it on again. At power-up, while the board charges its 136 µF, 2–3.5 A is drawn from the pack for a moment; a flat battery cannot deliver that. If it also happens with a full battery, the procedure in 10.5 (3 × 1 Ω series resistor).starts with a full battery
Charging (thermal rule)Lid closed, BATTERY OFFThe 18650's charging ceiling is 45 °C (60 °C when discharging). The box is closed and the thermal contribution of the ventilation is of the order of 1%, so whatever heats up inside ends up on the cell. Two rules: (1) do not measure while charging — with the board and the ESP32 off, the power going into the box halves; (2) the charging module itself heats up (TP4056 at 1 A ~1–2 W, at the bottom of the back wall). In a hot room (>30 °C) charge with the lid open. ⚠ This is a rule, not a CALCULATION: the temperature rise inside the box has not been measured. On the first charge put a thermometer inside, touch the cell body after 2 hours. Decision threshold: if the cell body goes from warm to hot under your hand (roughly above 40 °C, close to the 45 °C ceiling), switch to charging with the lid open (or halve the charging current: Rprog 1.2 kΩ → 2.4 kΩ, 0.5 A); if it stays at hand temperature, charging closed is safe and there is no need to measure again.ceiling 45 °C

Current and voltage measurement — connection

Battery capacity test — connection

Centre of mass — is the box balanced

  • Result: the box is balanced. The centre of mass is off the geometric centre by +5.5 mm sideways and -6.0 mm front-to-back (box 222 × 162 mm). No side is heavy: the two base rails carry 45% / 55% of the load.
  • Plenty of margin against tipping: the box does not tip over until it is tilted 53° in any direction (even in the worst case of the mass estimates, 42°). The centre of mass is 45 mm above the base, i.e. at 47 percent of the outer height — low.
  • The balance does not come by chance, but from two things: the box's own wood is 44% of the total and symmetric; and the heavy parts are on opposite sides (the main board on the left, the Q1 heatsink and the 18650s on the right).
  • Nothing was weighed — the numbers are estimates from volume × density or similar parts. That is why the audit also calculates every result for the worst case of the masses: it pushes each item to its limit in the direction that shifts the centre of mass the most and checks again. If you weigh an item, tell me: I update kutu_veri.KUTLE and regenerate the numbers.
  • What the criteria were: each rail carries at least 35% of the load (25% in the worst case), the centre of mass stays in the middle zone in depth, the tipping angle is ≥ 25° in every direction, the centre of mass is below half the box's height.
