Insulating coating (nail varnish / conformal coating)

ToWhenWhy
B — BOTH FACES of board B — the whole divider chain is on this boardBEFORE 6.3 (before the board goes into the box, easy to handle)The 6 × 820K series chain with its 617 → 103 V steps is on this board; leakage between neighbouring pads is both a safety issue and a RATIO error. The solder side comes first: that is where the leakage path is. The board's continuity/resistance checks must have passed; a probe does not contact a coated pad.
B — the solder points of the T_HV and T_N6 wires + the first 10 mm of the wireAFTER the wires are SOLDERED (solder them as pigtails before fitting the board)The highest (617 V) and lowest end of the chain. If the solder blob is not coated, the narrowest point of the leakage path is left exposed. Solder first, then coat — the other way round you have to scrape the varnish off.
Areas not to coat
Where NOTWhy
Board AIts highest node is 63.5 V (scope input) and its highest impedance 227 kΩ: 100 MΩ of surface leakage gives a 0.2% error, lost in the budget. Not needed.
Around the Q1 heatsink and the regulatorsNitrocellulose yellows and cracks with heat, and it also spoils the heat path. There is no high voltage there anyway: Q1 ≤ 38 V in the battery test, the regulators ±12 V.
Solder lugs of the panel jacks (CAL, BATTERY, LOAD, HV)The varnish cracks when the wire moves. There, heat-shrink or insulating tape is the right solution — the lugs are now far apart (B56/B58e), but the wire still moves.
Measuring points and test padsA probe does not contact a coated pad; do the gate measurements first.

4–5 thin coats, letting each coat dry (one thick coat traps the solvent inside). The coating stops surface leakage, not arcing through air — it does not replace distance. The real gain is accuracy: since the HV divider is 4.92 MΩ, surface leakage goes in parallel with the ratio (100 MΩ of dirty surface ≈ 4.7% reading error). If it has to come off, acetone removes it, but acetone also attacks some plastics.

Narrow clearances (< 6 mm, with a conductive side)

GapPairIs it a problem, what to do
0.54 mmB-foot1 ↔ ESP320.54 mm — the devkit's body can touch board B's wooden foot; it is an insulator, adjusted in place. The antenna is at this end, but ✅ CLOSED (user decision 2026-09-23): the internal antenna is a small tab the thickness of the board itself, the wooden block next to it is not a problem. Wood has low loss at 2.4 GHz and the whole box is wood anyway.
2.15 mmB ↔ HV anchor block2.15 mm — when board B was measured it came out 50×50 (the model was a 45.7-hole area), the gap to the anchor went down from 4.30 to 2.15. The anchor is in front of the board on purpose: when the HV cable is pulled, the cable tie resists, not the D8 joint. Wood, not a conductor.
2.15 mmB ↔ Q1 corner bracket2.15 mm — same reason (board B 50 mm). Q1's wooden corner bracket; the heatsink ITSELF is further away. A wood-to-board gap, no electrical risk.
3.82 mmB-foot2 ↔ RS3.82 mm — the shunt's body comes close to board B's wooden foot. The manganin U is in the air, it does not touch the spacer; the foot is an insulator, no problem.
4.00 mmA (empty edge) ↔ MT14.00 mm — appeared when board A went up onto 18 mm feet (user decision: the jumper wires underneath need 16–17 mm). The board's EMPTY BACK STRIP is now at z 18–20, the MT3608 at z 24–41: 4 mm remains vertically. The strip is bare perfboard and the MT module has an insulating body — they do not touch, only the margin got smaller. If needed, MT1 moves up one row.
4.09 mmA-foot4 ↔ B4.09 mm — board A's front-right foot and the body of board B. Both are fixed and the foot is placed in 6.1 by marking from the board, so it can be adjusted in place.
4.85 mmB ↔ ESP324.85 mm — appeared when board B was measured at 50 mm (the model showed 7.0 with 45.7). Not an electrical problem: the 617 V node is on the OPPOSITE edge of the board (orientation 270°) and its distance to the nearest conductor is 30 mm. The 4.85 mm here is board edge ↔ devkit body.
5.24 mmA-foot2 ↔ ESP325.24 mm — board A's wooden foot comes close to the devkit body; an insulator, adjusted in place.

Real 3D clearance (Euclidean), excluding the part's own carrier. The list is locked: if a new pair with a conductive side goes below 6 mm, the audit turns red. In addition 13 wood–wood pairs are below 6 mm — they are not listed one by one, they are trimmed in place with a knife; the audit only checks that they do not collide.
